* Products: Amazing range of products. And all of them are being inter-connected with one another leading to endless possibilities

* Pace: Company is moving at light speed in developing/acquiring/integrating new technologies in networking and other areas. If you are in the right group, the pace is blinding (in a positive way)
Cons:
* There are still some teams with very slow pace and not eager to change. But the culture is changing positively

* No free food. We have free snacks though. But honestly, free-food is over-rated!

Pros: Good coffee in the breakrooms.   Free popcorn.  Nice campus.   Remote chance of getting into good teams with competent managers.  But not likely.  Nice big buildings.   Big parking lot.
Cons: Ignorant and highly bureaucratic line-engineering organisation, which allows for dysfunctional team dynamic, constant turnover and stress.   Little to no innovation in products (Skype/Microsoft perfectly positioned to obliterate this "Telepresence" business with easier to use and less expensive products).  Creativity and innovation not valued, this company is a bone mill all about filling out forms.

Pros: Good place to start your career and to gain corporate experience. Benefits are slightly above average if you land the right position and the environment is extremely flexible when it comes to working hours.
Cons: It is an extremely political environment and individual contributors get their careers affected when they don't follow the game, sometimes without even realizing it. Executive leadership has developed this huge EGO that makes it practically impossible for the employee's feedback to be taken into consideration and make effective changes.

Pros: In the ios group for my internship at hq, it went very well.  Had a good manager.  Worked with people that great to work with.
Cons: Other location (Richardson for me) may be different.  For my full time offer I chose Richardson for a combination of cost of living and family living in the area.  All the good of the internship, the full time was opposite.  My manager had described his group as having what I wanted, but it wasn't close.  Not sure who to talk to, I spoke with the local choice program rep and was directed to another manager that just told I had to have been mistaken of the group I chose.  So I found another job and left, just before I left I found out that I should have talked to normal HR and not anyone from the choice program about the false advertising of my group

Pros: Lots of smart people that are mostly, very hard working. Good work/life balance (for most) with plenty of tools to help get that done. Pretty good benefits. Good lateral move possibilities.
Cons:
Stock options are worthless. Raises are few and far between and RSU (Reserve Stock Units) and cash awards are becoming more and more rare. Company is slowly evolving into IBM; people are commodities, everything is   assessed on cost/value and layoffs are a regular occurrence. Can't develop software products...horrible. 

Company is having a hard time realizing it isn't in a high margin hardware, "nobody ever gets fired for buying Cisco" kind of company. This is a big old supertanker and it takes FOREVER for it to change direction. Unfortunately most of its competition are in super fast speedboats.

Pros: Flexibility with work schedule and working from home is the biggest reason why people remain in Cisco.  Really good benefit package and you work with some great people and talent.
Cons: Switching off from work when you finish whether it's the end of the day or during your time off.  Management is frustrating, they just don't seem to see you as a person and recognize the employees that go over and above in their job. They complete leadership courses and you don't see any change in their management or leadership. The employees that are the loudest and boast about what they apparently do get the recognition.  Employees feel they are on 12 month contract with no job security.  Salaries are less than what you can get elsewhere.  Lots of great people leaving and it's not acknowledged why we are losing good talent and will continue to do so.

Pros:
Flexible work schedule, good benefits (health insurance and holidays), learning and development resources, approachable colleagues including those higher up the chain.
The company culture is good and they genuinely try to make sure that the employee is taken care of.
Cons: Lack of appraisals, hikes and promotions. Feels like people are given recognition based on their personal relationships rather than merit. Work is not challenging enough and it seems more like a beauracratic nightmare with so many approvals required for day to day work. Innovation sorely missing. Tendency of leadership team to speak in jargons and riddles with no clarity. Constant fear of job loss.

Pros:
Innovative products
Amazing customers
Useful experience
Great benefits, including child care
Market-value pay
Passionate collaborators
Cons:
Completely self-started, no support from management to get on your feet
Onboarding was the worst I'd ever experienced
No work-life balance, even though it is a touted benefit
Long nights, missing weekends
Forced office shutdowns that detract from PTO, so the PTO you get is actually get to use for yourself are a few days shorter than advertised.
Meetings and collaboration is so dysfunctional, even exec team warns employees that 'Cisco will consume you if you let it', yet you are penalized if you do not devote 24/7 of your personal life to the company.
No support from management when needed due to an optics-driven culture

Pros:
This might be a good company for someone who needs an average job that pays bills and doesn't bother too much. Ideal company to retire (or for already retired people).
People are nice and friendly, long holidays, good social activities and food.
Cons:
I completely wouldn’t recommend this company for recent graduates, adepts of new technologies, reformers and those who like challenges. It might be even dangerous for fresh people after university: you could pick-up outdated engineering practices and learn only re-invented wheels instead of modern tools. 

Regarding businesses itself, the company totally failed the opportunity when everyone switched to either hybrid or fully remote work. Ask yourself, have you ever heard about Webex at all (software or devices)? You might have heard about Skype, Zoom, even BlueJeans , but not about video conferencing devices developed mainly at Oslo, Norway.

I also want to highlight the following cons:
- missing onboarding process
- processes are vague in general
- close to zero internal documentation
- outdated technologies and engineering practices
- small R&D investments
- engineers with “senior” titles are weak as engineers
- communications between departments have seen better days
- politics, a lot

Pros: The quality and qualifications of Cisco employee is extremely high and the competitive atmosphere drives innovation, collaboration and working to "go the extra mile".   Cisco also drives a culture of fairness, diversity, collaboration and results that are "second to none".  We also have the most energetic and motivational CEO in the world!
Cons: The compensation is mediocre with base salaries just above the industry median and the stock is flat.  We are falling way behind the industry.   As mentioned many times, the company demands a lot out of its employees and the new culture of collaboration leads me to my day job of attending 6-8 meetings each day and my night job is reading email.  We are driving our business at break-neck speeds and I don't see the same focus and attention on the people aspect of the business as we did say 5-7 years ago.  It is a stressful environment to work in but I love my job.... sigh....  It's a company of many type A personalities.  Is the human body capable of keeping up this Cisco-pace?

Pros: If you want stability, good benefits, flexibility and management that is more likely to shuffle staff around than fire them, then this is the place.
Cons:
There is probably no money for fair raises and promotions because you were stupid enough to join Cisco directly, rather than a start-up that got bought out,
Too much critical software is farmed out to contract engineering firms with a questionable quality track record, you may end up constantly cleaning their mess,
Products have long lifetimes so there is a lot of legacy code and "historical reasons" for poor designs,
Project management is chaotic, 
Processes are paperwork heavy but still do not result in good documentation of software and designs,

Pros: There are still some talented people left, but most are actively seeking employment elsewhere
Cons:
Stock options are no longer issued.

Cisco has no formal management training program--and it shows.  Sales management consists of a bunch of idiots who are just political mafia players--very short on talent, high on themselves.  They treat their people so poorly that it is beyond me how Cisco can end up on anyone's "Best Companies" list.  

Pay used to be above market rate, but is now sub par.  Engineers are poorly paid, and sales goals are now very much unattainable from year-to-year.  Cisco is managing compensation via unattainable goaling.

Annual layoffs have absolutely demoralized the company.  The rank and file sales and engineering teams now worry EVERY DAY about looking good rather than doing the right thing for the customer.  It is a sad state of affairs.

Pros: Work remotely; make a real difference for over 70,000 employees by steadily improving internal systems. I'm lucky to work on something I love with a really fun and smart scrappy group. If not for this dynamic, would leave.
Cons: Annual Big Bang and continuous rolling layoffs is difficult; despite all the layoffs, headcount has held steady between 67k and 73k for the past decade - so the company is essentially at least attempting to let go of low performing individuals and groups to hire in growth areas while keeping control on cost. Despite best efforts on this, many good people get sucked back out to sea in these politically charged restructurings. RSU funding is extremely limited for my team, only top 5% (key performers) of individual contributors get any grants. IMHO, comp generally not competitive with industry. If you join Cisco, be super aggressive on negotiating on the way in - once you're in the system, even harder to move the needle on your base comp.

Pros: Great benefits, excellent work environment and peers--i never had any issues with any manager. The work flow is steady. Managers are smart. Frugal, but understand when money needs to be spent. Education their employees is important to them and they have a  pleathora of workshops to get engineers and managers up to speed. I love using their collaboration tools--they test products with their employees before sending them out customers. I think it's smart and increase our productivity. As a mobile worker, I find i spend more time working outside the office than at the office. Cisco is very flexible in how we work, and that improves how we live, play, and learn.
Cons: Lower than average salary for G&A. However engineers get paid very well. Upper level management communication is lacking which is directly correlated to its vertical hierarchy. Too many lines of management. 2500 directors in the company, i wonder how many managers there are.

Pros: Name recognition, good reputation, was once a meritocracy where pay and advancement were actually based upon your competence and contribution. Maybe it will be again, but not now.
Cons: Lack of innovation, arrogance when it comes to what customers want vs what thet R&D teams want to develop, huge growth of middle and upper management from other companies has ruined the once unique Cisco culture - making it just another big company. Continual empire-building with teams trying to rip off other teams. Lack of focus on the product. Lack of true leadership in the executive ranks at VP-Director level, especially in the Customer Advocacy/Service Provider LOB, where the execs seem more interested in 'going along to get along' rather than providing true vision or leadership. Some current cost-cutting measures have done nothing more than pass along Cisco's cost of doing business to their employees. Chambers has become very quiet and hands-off - I wonder what he thinks of what Cisco has become?

Pros:
Cisco is one of the best place to work. You would notice same company culture & standards all Cisco offices across the globe.  Cisco gives lot of important to its core values and ethics. You never notice partiality or unethical behavior in your day to day life over here. If you have offer from Cisco, there is no reason to think twice. 

Cisco pay lot of attention to employee benefits, it doesn’t need to  be always cash benefit, other benefits like health insurance, and bonus etc are best compare to industry.

Work life balance,
flexibility in work, 
Working from home, 
Technical exposure,
Great Leadership
Wonderful internal culture
Very relaxed work environment
Cons:
Pay is slightly lower than market,
Promotions and pay hikes takes longer than expected
Too Process oriented 
No travel opportunity

Pros: Large company that has a well-known name and a pretty comprehensive salary package.  There are some very bright people you will have the chance to work with in your role, and the company has some good CSR programs.
Cons: The company talks a lot about transparency but there is very little to none at this time.  Employees often can't tie their work to the overall goals of the company, typically because the goals are constantly in flux.  The promotion opportunities are unclear, as are the steps that you need to take to achieve one.  It is also a true matrix structure, which makes it very difficult in terms of dotted-line reporting relationships, lack of accountability, and being pulled in a lot of different directions.

Pros: Huge company, tons of info and knowlege to learn, great products, job can be interesting. Staff is varied and you might even find people you like. There are opportunities to grow if you stand out.
Cons: Lot of competition and back-biting, conceited employees who think they own the world just for working here (this was a shocker for me - I was not aware Cisco staff is superior). The demands are sky high and there is very little room for private life and work&life balance, if at all. Customers are absolutely first and you need to devote all your time to work if you want to bring the results and the figures you are expected to. The culture and the vision exists on paper but you will probably not notice any of the bla bla if you visit one of the offices. Management should not just preach but practice all the beautiful phrases.

Pros:
Excellent benefits (time off, crazy maternity/paternity leave, free college, etc), good pay, looks great on a resume. 

If you like working in TAC (support), you could do it until you retire. It's very hard to get fired.
Cons:
Getting a promotion or even a raise can be very difficult in TAC. If you are an innovative person, life at Cisco can be hard because Cisco wants you to be a cog in the machine. 

Teams in TAC with difficult to support products can find themselves overwhelmed with work, while teams supporting other products have nothing to do.

There are multiple customer service offerings at Cisco who's day to day job comes down to nagging TAC about support cases regardless of case progress/status.

Cisco wants to be agile like a startup but has too much overhead in terms of sticking to the status quo and propping up legacy business units to move quickly. 

There seems to be a lot of pointless changes that happen only to justify the existence of whatever team is responsible for making the changes.

Pros:
- Excellent infrastructure (workspaces/labs/IT support/TAC) to support engineers.
- Challenging technical work.Plenty of opportunities to work
   on problems faced by largest SP's and web OTT customers 
    like AT&T/Verizon/Facebook/google/amazon etc.
- Large pool of talented and experienced software
  and hardware professionals.
- Great access to cisco's global engineering talent.
- Mgmt largely expects and values initiative and self driven attitude
   from employees.
- *Only* Top performers well taken care of in terms of overall compensation,
   equity grants/bonus etc.
- Best employee transport system in bangalore.
- Flexi time.There is opportunity to achieve work-life balance.
   Looks like someone might pull the plug on this one soon :)
Cons:
-  Pay viz a viz competition needs to be reviewed.
-  Its not clear to employees whether management considers
    loyal long term employees as assets or liabilities :)

Pros: Best part is the flexibility if you're in a role that allows it, and most do.  Very strong brand with the enterprise helps drive the business as well as great solutions makes you a proud employee of Cisco.  People are nice and want to help, made lots of friends.  Great benefits depending on which region you're part of, but mostly ok stuff.
Cons: Can be more competitive in the pay, especially for internal employees... no one internally can get equity for switching positions but a new employee can and could come in and make same/more salary wise.  Lots of politics that is not needed and legacy policies and processes could use a revamp.

Pros: Cisco built the internet with no protocol religion, even though IP became the defacto standard. There is a lot of diversity in the company, both technically and culturally, which made it an interesting company to be part of. The international aspect of the company and the willingness to incorporate international values also contributes to the cosmopolitan feel of the company.
Cons: Parts of the business have become mature technology, and have lost their fun value. The grind of becoming the #1 vendor in many aspects of IT and Telecommunications has turned the exciting place to work, into a technology factory with little innovation and no radical thinking. Producing the numbers for the next quarter is more important than technical innovation or product development. Even the buildings in San Jose look tired and jaded now. Cisco talks about collaboration, it's the buzzword of the year, but very little collaboration exists within Cisco today, this is an empire of ivory towers.

Pros:
1) Work life balance
2) Pays Bonus even when the market might not be great.
3) Senior management is approachable.
4) Team members are generally and genuinely very helpful.
5) if you are working on a good projects the learning is simply too good.
6) Tech-talks, trainings and tech-related events are awesome.

Apart from the above, plenty of benefits such as. [listing few of them]
1) Company pays for Broadband @ home.
2) Flexible working hours [as long as work is not getting impacted]
3) Medicare and Annual health check-ups.
4) 'Superb' Cab facility.
5) Child care facility in the campus.
6) The Bangalore Campus is simply amazing. I've seen people coming to office on weekends to relax, walk, play and have fun.
Cons:
1) Off late too many organisational changes. [might be a good thing;  not according to me]
2) "Crying baby gets more milk" -- sort of a mentality. Hikes and promotions not always awarded per 'merit'.
3) Good amount of churn in the senior management suggesting things might not be that stable currently.
4) Most of the times your roadmap is not clear. Maximum visibility is I guess for coming 3 months.
5) Sometimes it is just fire fighting for weeks and months. Whatever comes up has 'ASAP' tagged to it.

Pros: Cisco is literally the company that made the internet - so it has some smart people and a huge customer & partner base. Work culture varies from group to group so it is hard to characterize it any one way.
Cons: The culture for Cisco has changed significantly from the 90s when it was a technology company singularly looking to get more market share with a variety of different technologies. Now the culture is primarily focused on politics. This feedback is primarily focused at Services and the culture there. A lot of the management is not barely familiar with the technology. When they get barely familiar with the technology, they are playing catch with where the market direction may be headed. Then there is complete ignorance of where the industry is heading with technologies such Virtualization, Analytics and Services in general. Management rewards each other with pats on the back and results of Services performance is not reviewed and weighed as a metric for evaluation. WIth the result innovation is stiffled.

Pros: Solid benefits, good pay.  You'll meet a lot of good people.
Cons: Management is weak.  Promotion from within is very much based on social connections not necessarily earned in every case.  Those promoted are not trained in managing people nor are they educated on company policy and process so when direct reports go to them for help it is seldom given.  The annual layoffs are unfortunately required as the company is poorly equipped to manage the bottom 10% out of the company, again, due to poorly trained managers and a weak performance management process.  I left on my own for a promotion but more importantly to feel valued, challenged and to get away from a really arrogant and incompetent management structure. I could have stayed and had the easiest pay check in the world but I respect my capabilities more than being a guy that fits the suit.

Pros: I joined Cisco straight from college in 2017, specifically the LIFT (finance rotation) program. This 2-year (four six-month rotations) program is a great introduction to the many functions within a global finance organization. I've felt empowered to explore the company with my own interests and passions in mind. Everyone holds the program in high regards, and it has been a great way to get leadership experience. Cisco's Early Career Network also invests in creating an environment of exploration and networking that fosters creativity and innovation within the many employees who are 1-5 years into their career at Cisco. Through this organization, I have had the privilege to connect with similarly motivated people all over the world!
Cons: Any global company comes with its bureaucratic challenges, but Cisco maintains a culture of curiosity and innovation that encourages growth throughout your career through challenging the status quo. Change takes time, but it starts here.

Pros: Great benefits, great pay, paid cell phone bill, remote work with occasional travel, stock plan, flexibility, steady compensation plan
Cons:
Not much work life balance- it’s very hard to truly be “off” when taking PTO
Not much diversity in sales teams- a lot of the reqs say “purple hair? Don’t care” when that is most assuredly NOT the case. 
Lots of changes are happening in the CX org without any clear path. You can’t implement changes without actual stepping stones to get there. It feels like we are working for a startup when Cisco has been around for 35 years now. 

They tend to bring in newer people at much higher salaries than those that have been within the company. This is common with a lot of companies, but it makes getting paid fairly compared to the market extremely difficult once you’re pigeonholed in a certain range

Pros: good work-life balance , pay , bonus
Cons: never know when they layoff

Pros: Breath of products, lots to learn about how technology solutions can be implemented.  Chamber is a very charismatic leader that always looks at possibilities; he as definitely a glass half-full exec. Also because there are many different functions, there are more opportunities to try different roles.  Health and medical benefits are still quite good(unfortunately employees are asked to shoulder more of the financial burden). The new health center and child care center is STATE of the ART.
Cons: Even though we have a great CEO, that charisma does not flow down to most of the executive team. It is a BIG & bureaucratic company now.  I was here during the late 1990s boom and a LOT has changed.  There's a lot of mid-managers that just suck the life out of you because they don't care about leading, rather they care about managing their own next promotion. Lots of "fringe" benefits that were part of Cisco are slowly being taken away (i.e., free sodas, company paid broadband, etc).  Those were nice while they lasted.

Pros:
Work environment is beautiful and well equipped.
Flexibility 
Stability
High Technology
Cons:
Management simply treats most engineers as replaceable.

Horrible management of software code base  with respect to customer releases results in poor usage of SW Engineers.  Most are getting burned out doing upkeep work and all new work seems to go to contractors.  

Management makes it known that engineers cannot be involved in business and completely shields them from any of it.

Pros: I worked for Cisco for 20 years, 11 months and enjoyed most everyday. I had a lot of opportunity to grow my talents and participate in making the internet what it is today. Worked many hours and traveled a lot but it was well worth it. Met a lot of great people all over the world.
Cons: After 20+ years I was all of sudden laid off along with 800 other employees. I was not given any opportunity to find another position or any reason why I was being let go. I was planning to retire in 4 years and now due to my age I am having a hard time finding a new job. Since the new CEO took over the company has gone downhill as far as loyalty to employees is concerned. Most people I know are always worried about being laid off. I would not recommend Cisco to anyone now as long as this culture persist.

Pros:
- Just brand name, legacy reputation, and big market capture in Networking domain. 
- It's a group of many small startups, say. So, if you fall in good BU, you will get good work, exposure, hikes, and live in peace.
- Nice clean big campus, facilities, gym, office infra.
- Pays huge to freshers from premium colleges, and to Senior Management.
Cons:
- Pays Low Salary as per market standard of Product companies. Lesser than some big service companies.  Always postpone yearly hike cycles by 1 or 2 quarters.
- Regular firing/LR.
- Too much work pressure. Too many product lines make it difficult to learn for Engineers. Customer escalations, bug counts are day to day worries. Very few old employees left who know product details, so no one is there to help.  
- Managers & Sr. Managers insulate engineers from Directors & VP who are real decision makers for hike & promotions. So mid-level engineers suffer from both side (lot of difficult work, and minimal hikes). Managers take credit & themselves get promoted.
- More suffering for people in Infra, platform, services, etc.

Pros: Cisco has a great culture - we encourage our employees to be active in their communities and to volunteer, we have a strong team environment, and we are encouraged to innovate and take risks.  We have great collaboration tools that allow many employees to work remotely and we do encourage work/life balance.  I love my team,  my peers and the future of Cisco as a leader in technology.
Cons: Learning to navigate your way around Cisco can be a challenge.  It is a very big and complex organization, but your teammates will help you! There are pockets of bureaucracy and legacy behaviors that we could improve on.  We need to integrate some of our tools and become more cutting edge.

Pros:
1. I experienced the most comprehensive training as a graduate. Before joined in Cisco, I know nothing about network and data center. Cisco invested on all CSAP to receive the best training in IT industry.

2. Work culture here is very open-minded. You can have happy hour with your manager and chat with your seniors. Any feedback is welcome in cisco. 

3. mentorship is a good culture in Cisco. My mentors are experienced sales. Besides the training content, my mentors' words are also important to me. Mentors' experience is the best local sales case study.

4. The whole CSAPers is a big family. you will have chance to know your colleagues from all over the world. I experience the family union culture in cisco. This is very very vital for young people especially for someone likes to social networking.
Cons: I work in APJC area, personally speaking, the business model is different from America. What you have learned in CSAP training will be probably a little different than the real world. But keep learning, don't settle!

Pros:
Cisco has many pros for working there which is due to the size of the company, they can offer great benefits
- Willing to hire new grads and give great new grad pay
- Great benefits, time off, time to give (40 hours), and baby leave
- They equip you with all the equipment you need to be successful
- Leadership is very open
- Laid off due to restructuring right before COVID-19 (Feb 25th) but they provided a tremendous package.
- Work/Life balance is great if you set boundaries.
Cons:
- The pay starts great as a new grad but is quickly average competitive compared to jobs area the area.
- Since the company is so large every position or opportunity you will see quite a bit of competition
-Quite a lot of change happening within orgs. Large company, so this is to be expected. However, about every year you will experience layoffs in some departments, new managers, etc.
- If you don't know how to network, learn it. That's the only way you can stand out in a company this large.

Pros: Cisco is a stable, very large company. Has a very good sales & channel organization; decent benefits. Talented resources if engaged properly.
Cons: Large company with too much political baggage. Employees & organizations that are not based in San Jose suffer from a compensation perspective, respect and career growth. The overall compensation of the company has suffered over the past 8-10 years as well. It appears to me that Cisco does not value it's experienced employees; hires too much from the outside in key positions without allowing experienced employees a shot at the promotional opportunity. "You're better off to quit, gain a more impressive title from a smaller company and then reapply to Cisco". Your chances of getting promoted are better using that tactic then trying to justify it internally.

Pros: Flexible work hours (opportunity to work from home if your manager allows it).  I found Cisco to be an intellectually stimulating work environment since most of my colleagues were very intelligent, hard-working, and collaborative.  There are some very interesting projects and many opportunities to learn new skills.  I had a great manager that offered opportunities to work on increasingly challenging projects if they were available and a person was performing successfully.
Cons: Senior management does not really understand what kind of resources are needed to implement some of these projects.  Some of the funding and staffing decisions that have been made have been disastrous to the successful outcome of projects, which can be measured by the quality of the implementation and number and severity of issues after Go-Live.  They do not understand that going live does not necessarily mean going live successfully.

Pros: Great brand name and strong foundation on what used to be a great company. Lots of flexibility if you have the right manager and can persuade them what you're doing is right. The opportunity to work with some very bright people (harder to find these days) and with leading edge technology. Open corporate culture.
Cons:
More redundancies creating a culture of fear and resentment. Job and career uncertainty by continual hiring freezes and arbitrary changes in expense policy. Sustained effective pay cuts such as reduction in restricted stock, no more company-provided internet, no more soft beverages, unreasonable goals (taxes) for technical people not based on merit. Reduction in hiring quality and talent recognition.

No one will tell you these are the glory days. They're long gone. This is a company that pretends to itself it's still cool and fun. But it really, really isn't.

Pros: Great people in some areas of the company. Good pay and benefits. Worked from home for over five years made for a great work-life balance. If you find the right group the work can be very satisfying.
Cons:
Too many people that don't contribute to the value of the company should be let go but the process for firing people takes 6+ months. Therefore, there are many people that are just moved around to avoid the firing process. Managers are "highly" encouraged to move people rather than fire them. Cisco seems to side with the bad employee for fear of reprisal and litigation.
Too many people caught up in following the "shiny ball" and not doing the right thing for the customer.
Little innovation from within the company. Difficult to get promoted unless you have a technology background.
Cutting free soda seemed like a good idea from a cost standpoint but had a greater negative impact on moral. It's the little things.

Pros: The opportunity to move around within the company in different roles is something that you don't find at many companies, however that comes with a con (see cons below). The pay and benefits are pretty competitive as I'm finding out and the flexibility to manage work/life is key but you pay for that in other ways (see cons below).
Cons: Constant org changes usually lead to opportunities but they also lead to confusion and politics. Your boss and organization can change 4-5 times over as many years but your role stays the same. The global nature of how Cisco is structured makes it an interesting place to work but depending on your role you can be working 24x6 as you have to satisfy Europe, Asia and US timezones which necessitates you to work through the evening every night just to catch up.

Pros:
Good people- majority of my managers and employees have been smart and self motivated.  People care about their jobs, care about their co-workers, care about the community.

Love the moto:  "Best in the world, Best for the world".    Relentless focus on execution, without losing need to do good in the world.  

Great work-life balance.  Employees work hard, but flex time is the norm.  Very common to have 7am calls, 7pm calls, but also ok to be coaching soccer at 4pm, or at doctor's appt with your mother in the middle of the day
Cons:
Many people have been here a long time- there's a sense of entitlement amongst those here 20+ years.  Some complacency, related to above.

Hard to move up- promotions to director level and above seems to require inside connections.

Pros: Cisco is a great company to work for in the sales force if you are seeking autonomy and are a self starter.  The more responsibility you seek, the more you will get.  They are also big on using their own technology to collaborate and complete your daily work.  They are also big on information exchange and internal education - there is usually more technical content that one can absorb.  Overall, I think Cisco sales is a good place to work!
Cons: over the period of time I have been with Cisco, I have seen the layers of management grow and the result has made for a lengthy process to get things accomplished.  The continued thickening of processes and procedures is certainly slowing everything down.  One can spend more time on internal meetings than doing what we were employed to do - sell.  Cisco is also no longer the best in compensation, it hands out fewer and fewer RSUs and the raises are in the single low digits.  As you get closer to the top of the SE pyramid, opportunities for promotions are far and few between.

Pros:
Extremely flexible employment, also means you are expected to work anytime, everytime. Still, being able to work from home, from a cafeteria, or from another country's Cisco office is great.
A lot depends on who your direct manager is, whether they support and promote you or aim to exploit and ditch you once you got burned out. Dynamic environment. Ability to work with the newest gadgets. Some nice people, some .ssh..es, as everywhere.
Cons: Work is nonstop, no time off - they call it work-life balance, but this is actually working all the time. You are the coolest if you join videoconference meetings from your annual holiday on an island. Actually happens. Pay is relatively OK so most people tend to work as hard as they can while the income lasts, as you can never be sure whether the next reorg will get away with you.

Pros: Cisco pays pretty well and offers good flexibility and some perks, and some of the administrative things work surprisingly well for such a giant corporation.  Cisco does a lot of good work in the community and encourages staff to give back to various charities, etc. and does a good job of promoting mobility across job functions, etc.
Cons: There is a constant threat of a "Limited Restructuring" - nearly every year, you will lose some colleagues if not your own job, which absolutely kills morale.  They make a lot of noise about how great their culture is - which if you have to say it so often, means it is likely not the case.  They can be completely tone-deaf, for example, scheduling all-hands, AMA-type town-hall meetings with execs on the same days they're laying off hundreds of people, making "The People Deal" complete BS.

Pros: You're given the tools you need to do your job and you're entrusted to "do the right thing" (that was in the orientation).  There's a complete absence of micromanagement -- no one will tell you what to do, though they will sometimes provide guidance if asked, or as part of regular team operations.  Work/life balance is great; everyone is given a CVO to support working from home, which can be expected when you're working with teams all around the world.
Cons: Everyone is doing their own thing.  Sometimes the pieces come together to make a functioning product/service, but only at the lowest levels.  The higher you go, the less likely it is that what you're working on will play nicely with what someone else is working on, and there is little broad leadership to tie all of the pieces together.

Pros:
I worked at Cisco in RTP for a few years. Over time it become obvious that my project peers were working other full-time jobs and shouldering me with an unfair amount of project burden. I made management aware of this issue but they were too busy to effectively look into the matter. It was a complicated issue; management typically doesn't have time to manage staff at Cisco and actually see whats going on. Many managers have too many employees, some like mine have the title of manager but are really too busy working a sales role. This puts them in the place of trusting mid-level employees.If your under a shady one theres not much you can do.
It got very shady in my exit interview when no HR representative was present. In lieu of that I was given a web form to fill out.

Pros: Great opportunities do exist. as with most large companies Its really a roll of the dice as to who you work for.
Cons: As stated the cliques and poor ethics that grow in certain areas.

Pros: Work from home, competitive pay, market leader in everything
Cons: Too many all hands calls to bash white people and scream racism. In your face die hard liberal leadership. Gave $1M to BLM. CEO recently said we don't want your thoughts and prayers they don't work anymore. We need to take action. This in regards to recent violence in the US. Desperately anti gun. Blindly follows anything Liberal politicians tell them to with no regard to other views. Publicly bashed white people, Republicans, pro 2nd amendment employees, and likened them all to terrorists and racists!

Pros: Big brand name. Good team
Cons: No job security. Rest everything is ok.

Pros:
Many of the people I worked with were friendly and helpful
You were given the resources needed to do your job -- a decent laptop, phone, etc.
Lots of career mobility if you are a full time employee 
Training opportunities were available, even for contractors (!)
Nice campus with decent amenities for a company of its size (gym, cafeteria, etc.)
Cons:
More meetings than you can possibly imagine
Inconsistency between departments on how employees/contractors were treated 
Contractors are not given feedback on their performance until too late 
"Cisco Rule" applied randomly inside company -- some groups kept everyone year after year while others laid off their entire staff for almost no reason
Poor employees often manage to squeak through the cracks while good ones get terminated
Simple projects often become unnecessarily complex because of the need for consensus by EVERYONE.
Extremely big company -- very easy to sit in an environment and not know who your neighbors are or what they do for years unless you introduce yourself to them

Pros: Still a decent name to have on your profile, pay is still ok, but dropping fast. Plenty of internal training resources and focus on being a good workplace
Cons:
Though they'll claim otherwise, the culture is all about the sale, leaving the technology on the back burner. Of course the majority of the sales staff have limited tech capability anyway, so they wouldn't know the difference. But in spite of all the talk of innovation and disruption, it's just that - talk. The product suite is ageing and there's little on the horizon to address that. Much talk about programmability, yet a huge percentage of the company doesn't have the most basic of coding skill, which shows painfully in the work product.

Salaries are diving, advancement is hindered by significant headcount pressure in many regions. Country director up seems to see the market for what it is, but most people below that are hiding their heads in the sand or at war with some other business unit. Lots of talk about transparency and open feedback, but nobody is actually interested in hearing anything that doesn't confirm their existing view.

Pros:
• Work-life balance is prime here and everyone respects people’s personal time
• Culture is fairly nice and open. Not cutthroat
• Great for anyone looking for a stable, predictable job — especially good for people taking care of a family (onsite daycare, maternity + paternity leave, etc)
Cons:
• Salary negotiation is non-existent if you are hired through the university program. Really. Nor is team matching.
• Promotions are rare and are often based on inter-company politics. When they are awarded, they are underwhelming and don’t match the local rent inflation
• RSUs are very rare and, again, very political / based on team+BU
• There is always talk about innovation by the leadership, but the culture is fairly stale as are the products, so opportunities for innovation are few and far between
• No free food or snacks. A couple of buildings do have free snacks, but it was for a “beta snacks program” that was never spread company wide.

Pros:
worked here for 4 years and quit to progress my career:
1. Work life balance is great. 
2. A lot of the people are really fun and there's definitely a lot of help if you need it. 
3. Really open to learning and continuing your learning
Cons:
oh man after 4 years you definitely start seeing the cracks:
1. Open discrimination against men is pretty tolerant here, I.E. opportunities and events only women can attend and sign up here.
2. You're underpaid from day 1,  don't expect that to change, the next year's new grads will come in at a higher pay than you.
3. Career progression doesn't happen too often, you'll definitely get the work but never the monetary or career recognition.
4. Some pretty toxic LGBTQ+ people I.E.  I was told it was "good that I was discriminated against because I'm not a minority."

Pros:
Telecommuting is encouraged
Teams are competent and unified
Internal transfers are easy
Code ownership is shared to relieve pressure against vacations
Training and higher education is supported
Cons:
Micromanagement is rampant and backed up by a culture of fear

External tools are poorly chosen, overvalued as silver bullets, and not optimized to fit the needs of developers

Employee evaluation system is based on an individual's reputation for working long hours, oratory skills in meetings, powerpoint skills in presentations, and popularity with upper management

Advice of developers is disregarded by technical leads and managers, yet failure is always attributed to a lack of effort and communication among the team

Project marketing and team size are used as leverage among management, leading to unhealthy competition between teams, code redundancy, and useless features creeping into requirement lists

Hard work is not rewarded as much as shameless self promotion and socializing outside the office

Deadlines and milestones are decided without any input from developers implementing the requests

Pros:
Good company name on your resume, recruiters will try to snatch you up if you start looking for another job outside the company.
Engineers know their stuff well
Lots of perks (CAP awards for a project well done, good onsite cafeteria, gym, etc)
Company has many business units covering many technology areas
Cons:
sweat shop: expect 70+ hours of work regularly if you are an engineer.
high pressure: not only do you have to put in long hour, it is a high pressure environment. Every one is pressuring everyone else to get the work done, leading to a very nasty environment and teamwork suffers a lot. People just do not have time to help others unless it is something that is "visible" by their management.
Company frugality policy means you do not have the resources (equipment) to actually do the work expected of you. People spend a lot of wasted time fighting over equipment and making do with prototype that do not work.

Pros:
- Working environment is excellent - facilities are modern, always being updated, refreshed
- Use of technology - webex, telepresence, unified comms makes it easy to work with virtual teams
- Good opportunities and challenges - able to make a difference
- Can over achieve on your bonus if company overachieves
- Stock awarded for good performance
Cons:
- Progression in terms of pay and promotions is far too slow - lots of people waiting to get to the next level, management don't deliver on commitments, unclear and inconsistent promotion process
- Reward & recognition is inconsistent - some rewarded for doing little, others nothing for doing a lot
- Too much complexity - strategy, systems etc - undergoing major simplification effort now but a little too late
- Pay rises only when the company has made it's numbers (even through inflation has gone up and the company has huge cash reserves)

Pros: Overall, the employees are committed and want to do the right thing; however it is not clear from the executive management team that they are doing the right thing by the employees.  Many people and even some executives are trying to preserve the core culture of what made Cisco a great company to work for.  They have several great benefits and given the right organization, a sub-culture that you can learn and grow, but have a long ways to go to get the human back in HR and across the company.
Cons: Cisco's culture is about respect and care for each other and always doing the right thing, but you find several incidents where respect and care is only for those in the inner circle and you will find several executives not always doing the right thing for the environment, company, culture or it's employees

Pros: Old glory of networking protocol patents and acquisitions (of IP) is pretty impressive
Cons: This is by far the worst place I have worked. I have been in silicon valley for 2 decades and worked at many places. Joined Cisco recognizing it will be a great place. Hardly. Not sure if only my Manager but he was a jerk. The communication between groups & within groups is awful. There are many cliques and if you fit into one of them, it does not matter what you do - you will move ahead. The source code is not shared between groups - meaning you have no access to the source code or their design documents of the group you are working with. You can get it through unofficial channels through acquaintances. Remember cliques. Many details are kept secret and internal management conflicts are too much. The management in many cases is unethical and force you to work on weekends. Hire cheap labor from abroad and ask you to train them. This is the only place where I noticed the Manager expects the outgoing person to work until his/her last day. Above all, the technology they are working with is dated is not worth staying here for anything. Unless you can't find a job anywhere else.

Pros:
- Looks great on a resume; employers love to hire ex-Cisco employees
- Great benefits
- Many co-workers are smart; some are very smart indeed!
- Much of the employee education is top-notch
- Flexible work hours and work-remote policies
Cons:
- A bad manager can really make things terrible, and there isn't really anything you can do about it; bad managers tend to stay in place indefinitely, unless they quit
- Salary is generally below-par
- Stock price has been flat, so options and ESPP aren't worth much
- Major changes in direction come as a surprise to rank-and-file employees.  Your business unit could be shut down at any time, and you could wind up moving somewhere completely unrelated
- A very large organization generally means lots of process and lots of red tape
- Cisco has apparently started doing annual layoffs, dumping 10%-20% of their employees each time.  Morale problems are endemic in part as a result of this

Pros:
- Great pay
- Awesome team of resources available to help you get the job done
- Due to of the size of the company and the "human network", your ability to move around when needed/desired is incredible
- As long as you are making your number, you have full autonomy
- Great benefits and perks
- Working for the leader in the industry is never a bad thing
Cons:
- Because you have a quota, it can sometimes be difficult to take advantage of the awesome PTO - Cisco AM's tend to always be ON, which can be a challenge in the area of work/life balance
- You MUST find the right team and right manager, otherwise your success can be limited
- If you are not on the right (inclusive) team, it is possible to get lost in this BIG COMPANY and feel like just a number
-

Pros:
Excellent Bonus, Good work life balance, flexible timing, work-from-home, No desktops at all, everyone gets laptop.
Great resting place between two demanding jobs, may be for an year or two
People including Managers are very good, treatment of employees is very good
Cafeteria facilities are very good, at least in Cessna Business Park which houses Cisco's own campus.
Transport facility is there at a reasonable price for permanent employees, contractors can avail of it but pretty expensive for them.
Easy hiring for contractors, the process is tougher for permanent employees
Cons:
Not a great place if you are career-oriented.
Things move too slowly, and hardly anything ever gets done
Vision and Strategy is missing for most BUs. No long-term thinking.
Stay longer, and employability outside decreases phenomenally
Ad-hoc, difficult-to-explain firings (not necessarily bad performers)
Promotions are very difficult. 
Un-organized hierarchy, nobody know which designation is senior or junior, or who falls where.
No HR involvement once you get hired, they only recruit you after that they never check on you. 
Contractors to Permanent Employees ratio is approx 8:2 (this could be BU specific), and hiring of contractual workers is very lenient, so you end up with lots of poor performers.

Pros: If you're willing to work around the clock (I have a 1AM-6AM meeting tomorrow, and another on Sunday) you can do very well at Cisco.
Cons: Cisco has gone to a "management by council" mode so nobody seems to have accountability anymore.  Chambers and team seem to be floundering, badly, after making some really bad decisions that they now have to rectify.  Rumor has it huge layoffs are coming soon, and budgets are being slashed in really scary places.

Pros:
- Portfolio of products/services and sales force are a juggernaut
- Incredibly strong financial position
- Competitive total compensation
Cons:
- Lack of vision and 'old school' leadership
- Higher priority on balance sheet than it's people and developing a compelling vision
- Direction is to grow in China, India, etc. and Outsourcing. Quality of some products and services are noticeably lower.
- Lost it's appeal and growth potential due to above

Pros: Competitive Salary and bonus plan although bonuses are rarely paid unless you can walk on water.
Cons: Uses Bell Curve to force those rated as lowest are placed on probation or terminated, those in the mid 74% range get patted on the head and told try harder next time, and only those in the top percentile get raises, perks, bonuses, and or promotions. Sounds like a great incentive plan until you realize that out of 100 people every year roughly 14% have to be put on probation and a percentage of those have to be terminated. My former manager is a bigot and sexist so he used his power to drive people out he didn't approve of and with a PC approach to justify his racism and sexist views. Hopefully HR has outed him for what he is and he isn't bullying people anymore. But Crisco promotes these values from my experience and rallys around such people at management levels so work as hard as you may your number will eventually be up, unless you're the Sociopath that can manipulate the system in your favor.

Pros: Cicso has a good benefits package and they have $$ in the bank.  I think of them as IBM of the 1990's -- No one was ever fired for buying Cisco.  You start with 20 days of PTO a year.
Cons:
IMHO, Routers/switches have become commodity  products.  Years ago, cisco had a sufficient technology lead that they could charge premium.  Today, they are marginally better, if that.

Not an easy place to work.  Engineers were given responsibility without Resources/empowerment.  Big company politics in place.  It felt that you are on call 24x7.  Significant development efforts in India Yearly focal reviews put you in competition with your peers, resulting in subtle anti-colaboration.  There is not a lot in innovation coming from the company.  Cisco Buys new technology. 

Development is process burdened.  

There is little respect for Seasoned professionals, company has been pushing to get young talent and push out
experienced engineers.  Seems to me that this is a "bean counter" approach with the assumption that all bodies are equal.

Pros: Cisco campuses have many amenities. There are many ways that you can stand out. They have a large infrastructure which can be supportive. Teams are open and friendly to new people and it is easy to make friends if you come with an open attitude.
Cons: Cisco is an enterprise! There are so many departments within Cisco that no one knows or often dares to ask what they do. Often part of your job might be researching what departments and who are is in charge of the elements you have the responsibility of improving or changing. In some departments they are just now embracing Agile development. Alas to do so they are using multiples of online tools that don't interact with each other. It seems most departments prefer using spreadsheets that are not live or shared and have to be updated by every member of the team to 'stay up-to-date'.

Pros: Excellent benefits and starting pay is competitive.
Cons: Raises are almost non-existent.  Raises do occur, but they seem to be only for a small section of employees at the absolute top of the performance scale or who have made the right impression with senior leadership.  So you can do a great job and not see a penny more for 3 or more years.  So while the world becomes more expensive to live in, you are are having less an less expendable income.  If this methodology resulted in more job security it would be worth it, but it is just Cisco's normal business model to force management into stack ranking exercises to determine who could be fired.  Also, Cisco does not value most experience gained outside of Cisco.  So you may have years of experience coming in the door, you will not be considered for promotions until you have gained the same experience under Cisco.

Pros:
Cisco is not only the greatest place to work at, but in fact, it is the greatest place to live your life - by learning, innovating, creating, sharing, leading and building an impactful and successful life - personally & professionally, for yourself and for others around you. 

I have been at Cisco 12 yrs+ now and worked in 2 different continents and 5 different teams and I am as enthused , excited and grateful for each day at work (if not more), as I was when I started. 

As a woman, as a professional, as a human - I have felt supported, encouraged, valued and challenged to be the best version of myself - through the experience, exposure and education opportunities I have been equipped, enabled and empowered with.

All I am and all I hope to be ...I owe to Cisco and the people I work, live, learn, play, innovate and give back with.
Cons: We are making big strides in promoting women to leadership roles across all ranks and there is more to be done with great initiatives like Multiplier Effect and Multiply Tech Diversity initiatives.

Pros:
- industry leader, strong product pipeline, and install base
- flexibility in virtual office is part of culture- work from home is a nice perk
- team selling where product specialists are there to support sales and front-line management (i had a great manager) was always supportive to cut thru red-tape to get deals done
- sales driven culture where account managers are given the independence to run territory as needed
Cons:
- quotas are driven by much more than just % of expected growth-heavy favoritism in who get the best territories and hold-over accounts to the point that if you are not "in the inner circle" it will be hard to hit your quota 2 years in a row
- management unrealistic expectations about new products (ex. UCS product line)
- multi-tiered hierarchy where it is hard to move into new roles even with strong performance
- looking like the next HP and many perks have been cut and employee retention is getting to be a problem

Pros: Lots of really smart people with good salaries and benefits. Cisco is still light years ahead of a lot of companies and that allows you to be able to move to other companies fairly easily after you've workes at Cisco. Also, being able to move around within the company used be a lot easier to do, but the last few years has been really locked down.
Cons: Marketing (Operations specifically)- Management is terrible and one director in particular is completely unprofessional and has burned out a number of high quality employees. The result is a huge turn over rate in Operations and in Marketing as well. The senior management seems to allow it to continue. The result is a very negative environment with no career growth.

Pros:
Great company, great leadership and lots of potential.  Individuals are truly regarded based on their merits and little or no weight is given to gender. 
Women occupy leadership places in all areas; not only those generally reserved for women (HR, Marketing) but also sales and engineering.
Cons:
That being said, it is a white, male, sales dominated company and that is a very powerful legacy that is hard to break away from. From the "play" events (Golf, Vegas etc), to the silly badge clips that only work with belt loops, everything still screams "we cater to men".  It's not malicious and change is coming but it's hard and it will take time. 
Also, parental leave is pathetic. As a CA company it should follow CA law, instead the follow whatever minimum is required by law in your state which makes it very unfair for non-California moms. In most states fathers get no leave and need to use their vacation time.

Pros: This is a big company with a lot of great employees and a lot of innovation.  Cisco does not want to join the long list of previously great Silicon Valley companies that missed a market transition.  They are constantly trying new strategies (which gets a little exhausting at times, throwing stuff at the wall and seeing what sticks).  I think the salary, bonus, and RSUs for top performers are very strong.
Cons: 2005-2014 I thought Cisco was a great place to work, but not a good stock to own.  Now it is kind of the opposite.  If your Business Unit is not growing by 10% annually, you will get your budget cut proportionally and that money will go to the growing BUs.  Our BU growth slowed, and we got cut a little in 2014, a LOT in 2016, and now again in 2017 including me.

Pros:
The work /life balance is fantastic. I'm able to work from home whenever I'd like, and since Cisco is a global company, I've been able to travel on my own and work out of other Cisco offices without taking time off.    

5 days of paid time off to volunteer. 

The people! Everyone I've worked with has been very nice and eager to share knowlege.  

On campus gym and doctors office at a very reasonable price. 

Dogs can come in the office on Wednesdays and Fridays.
Cons:
There's no IT training program for recent grads like there is for sales and HR. 

Initial team placement after recruitment was off, but I was able to rotate into an area that I'm really excited about after about a year. 

Continuous layoffs really impact office morale.

Pros: Pay on par with many other large companies along with decent benefits. Good co-workers and talented individuals in certain areas.
Cons: Cisco has seemed to forget about their employees in the sense of that their employees are just that employees, they have a life outside of the realm of Cisco. Forced PTO at the holidays (taking six forced days when the PTO is limited in comparison to other companies) was certainly intrusive. In addition to the company's stance on mandated vaccination status was also aggressive without many exceptions. If you don't agree with the views of the leadership team you are silenced. Not a place I wanted to stay and I would encourage others to seek companies that respect personal boundaries.

Pros:
Great benefits
Good people
Have all the tools I need
Excellent review process
Great bonus system
There are ample opportunities to grow, and management within the CHS business unit at least listen to you
Cons:
HR when we were Scientific Atlanta was very good.  HR at Cisco is not as responsive.
IT support has just been decimated with the latest restructuring (Aug 2011).  It's all done now by telephone support from a remote location.
SPVTG does not yet have a clear path.  However, senior management of the group has recently been changed, and these problems may be corrected. Change was indeed needed.

Pros: Very flexible work environment: working from home is easy as is taking time off. Initial on-the-job learning is good and the networking software development experience gained was valuable. Enjoy working with helpful colleagues.
Cons: Compensation growth is mediocre and I do not see people getting adequate reward for performance from management. It may be the nature of the game but there is no cohesiveness in the execution of goals and deliverables. There is always a last minute scramble to push products out, and there are too many branches and people touching the same code for clean code development. No encouragement for training and personal development from management, you have to push it on your own.

Pros: You are able to work with some of the best and smartest folks in the industry. Compensation is good and and opportunities to advance are available, even though competition is tough. The company knows how to align employee behavior with the goals of the company.
Cons: It is a "Hero-to-Zero" company. Come end of July the latest, expect major shifts in focus areas, responsibilities, expectations. In sales, do expect your targets to go up in a way that makes you ask "How possibly can I achieve that ?". Feature velocity in products sometimes low as there are sometimes too many diverging interests.

Pros:
leader in networking area
flexible working hours and relaxing (sometimes layback) working environments
starting salary is reasonable for new graduate
Feel like home environment for foreign workers (70% of engineers are Asian.
Many executives (directory, VP) are Asian (mainly Indian).
A lot of talents in networking area.
A great place for Assurance engineers or managers (QA) because the pay is the same as other developer or managers, no discrimination like other companies.
Cons:
The pay raise is crawling slow.
Need to fight with others most of the them.
A lot of overlapping products among different departments
Layoff is an annual ritual
Constantly outsource jobs to other countries like India, China, Russia.
Not enough talents in new technology.
Buy company instead of building, most of the work is integration, not much learning (waste of time) unless you work for the acquired companies.
Lack of internal documents on design, implementation due to job security for engineers and managers.

Pros: There's a lot of opportunities at this enormous global company with fantastic benefits - but no one is going to hand hold you to develop your career. It's really easy to get paid well, work 9-5 and be at Cisco for a decade, if you want a mommy-track or low key job. If you want to learn, be challenged, move up fast, learn the org landscape, find the right sponsors and there are lots of interesting learning experiences to be had.
Cons: Political, big and slow in many parts of the org. Back channel negotiation and side discussions are required to smoothly get stuff done, and not doing so has career ramifications. That said, if you understand the landscape, you can do well. Had great experiences and career development, but ultimately I left because I wanted more direct impact than what I could see as a cog in the massive machine that is Cisco. That said, it was worth the tour of duty

Pros: Cisco Systems at RTP by far has been one of the best experiences.  The University Experience team and made the process seamless. As an intern, onboarding week made me feel comfortable and welcomed with open arms. The opportunities at Cisco Systems are endless. With the love and support of my colleagues, I was given the opportunity to learn about myself, team work and why Cisco Systems is the #1 Technology company in the world. My projects were challenging and one-one-one sessions with key stakeholders in the company were engaging as well. I was given the opportunity to solve one of Cisco's problems and present my findings to management, and the VP of my org. Definitely my best internship by far and would recommend the company to others. I have chosen to stay at Cisco for my first post-college career position.
Cons: Not so much of a bad thing, but Cisco is what you make it! It is completely up to you on how your career will be at the company.  I have learned this very quickly in my internship and will be keep it with me as I begin full-time.

Pros: Great company. Great work culture. Highly talented people. The company provides opportunities for growth, career transitions, mentoring. I mean it's up to the employee to make the best use of the opportunities available. I got my immigration work also done by Cisco. Even after I left Cisco, I got support from Fragomen. I must say I am very very impressed by the way Cisco takes care of their employees and former employees.
Cons: I don't like the new open workspace concept. It's very chaotic and highly unproductive. Most of the employees at Cisco don't like it. I didn't meet anyone who liked it. But still, it was enforced. It was disappointing to see Cisco didn't care about employees opinion. I can understand that it's highly cost-effective to stuff double the employees in the same old space.

Pros: Great starting point for your career. Working here sharpened my professional skills to get me ready for my next step.
Cons: Turning inside Account Management role into a call center. Management is all about politics and the "it" groups. VERY much like high school. Going in and getting the job done doesn't cut it anymore. You have to make sure you're one of the "popular" ones to get promoted, or to keep your job. I watched multiple colleagues that couldn't cut it in multiple positions be moved around from one job to another all while making better money than the person next to him or her that is hitting goal, not making as much money, and who will be let go before the person being shuffled around. If you have an opinion, make sure you DON'T go to management about it, showing you have your own thoughts only puts a target on your back. I have never seen so many backstabbers in my life.

Pros: You will be working mostly in cutting edge technology. Very rarerly people has to work on older technology. You will get to know the complete networking domain expertise exposure. Limitless learning opportunities - on demand video lectures, soft skill development opportunities - unlike other companies in Cisco this is not restricted. It is upto you to utilise. Other companies it depends on managers. Top level management is very good and the open culture and the work environment is awesome.
Cons: You have to manage and uplift your self - both time management, career, work life balance etc. No body cares. Managers care only your work completion. Too many emails - you like or not daily must to waste 2 to 4 hours time in emails. If your manager is not good then you will be in trouble to complete your task in time.

Pros:
- I learned a tremendous amount during my time with Cisco
- Benefits are pretty good, better than most other companies in my geographic area
- Opportunities for internal movement
Cons:
- Leadership tolerates drama, lying, backstabbing
- Lack of accountability for managers and individual contributors
- Star players are often invisible to management, even their own managers
- Old fashioned office politics are strongly encouraged and required above a certain level
- It's often the most destructive employees who get the most positive attention (squeaky wheel gets applauded when they fix things they broke?)
- Very short term memory of cause-and-effect consequences (same mistakes made repeatedly by leadership)
- Self-centered culture, cliquish, judgmental and eager to exclude from the "in" groups
- Very much a sink-or-swim organization, but talent is valued less than "playing the politics game"
- The organization will consume your life if you let it, some managers don't accept that you have a life outside of work
- Manager's word always taken as solid gold by leadership
- Overall very toxic environment

Pros: It has very Good workplace facilities
Cons: No regular hike cycles yearly

Pros: Opportunity to work on great technology. In addition, the executive management is the best I've seen in working for various companies in Silicon Valley. Flexible work hours (though you need to work extremely hard). Varied set of products, so if you get bored doing something, you can move to something completely different without changing jobs.
Cons:
Pay is not great: especially if you've been around for some time. Newcomers get paid market rates, while old-timers struggle to get raises.
Raises are hard to come by, and are highly dependent on your manager and group. 

Middle management sucks. The executives are excellent, and their strategic vision has kept Cisco going, however, there's an enormous amount of deadwood,  that needs cleaning. Too many directors sit around doing nothing and don;t get fired, in some ways its like getting tenure at Cisco to become a director.
A lot of engineering will probably end up being moved to India, so watch out. 
Has gotten fairly bureaucratic, so getting things done is hard.

Pros: If you like working countless hours on things that often are more political vs. meaningful, then this is the place for you.  If your career is your life, then this is the place to dive in and see where it takes you.
Cons: Too much CYA required.  Management sees what it wants to see and often recognizes ones who are better political contributors rather than true work contributors. Work-life balance doesn't exist if you want to survive.  The political side of Cisco came to the surface during/after the 2001 layoff.  It has thrived since.  Finally training of new managers has only just begun.  Promoting someone from within to management (who has never been a manager before) is a gamble. Training is not adequate.  Thus many employees suffer.

Pros: As an engineer I think some of the best reasons to work for Cisco is the opportunity to work on a wide variety of technologies.  In my business unit (GSBU), people do have the freedom to work on technologies that they find interesting.  Also, the stability of working for the industry leader is nice.  In some ways, the benefits are better than any other company I have worked at (4 weeks of vacation).
Cons: Recognition and promotions are difficult to come by.  It seems as if promotions have more to do with "ass kissing" than merit or accomplishments.  Also, it's not likely that you're going to make rapid career advancements.  This is a big company with a pecking order in place.  If climbing the career ladder quicker is your priority, Cisco (or any large company for that matter) is not your place.

Pros: Great benefits, resources, and the network. One of the best place to intern or do a 6-month co-op as an engineer.
Cons:
Large corporation. Easy to get lost in the crowd of people with similar skills. Bad communication amongst different department and business units.

I was hired as a Hardware Engineer intern for the "Cisco Choice Program." The uniqueness of the program is that if you do well during your internship you will get hired back and get to interview the managers of different business units within Cisco and pick which Business Unit you want to work for.

Due to the bad economy and higher ups decisions, they decided to cut all hardware engineers position for the Cisco choice program leaving only Software and MBA students.

Pros: Finally they have some good products and it's nice to work for a leader. You have the ability to learn new technology's, to be part of the a world wide virtual team. You have the ability to learn new stuff, to work in a motivated team and to be part of this culture.
Cons: There is NO work-life balance! Of course, they saying that you take your private time, but they give you workload up to 60-70  hours per week. Where is there the work-life balance or at least the possibility? The management is just thinking from quarter to quarter. Just number are important, nothing else. Ethic exist just at the paper. For the salary there is downwards trend. Meanwhile there are trying to remove all the benefits. They are just selling the future, a lot of the products are not ready or poor. Meanwhile the company is to large for fast moves. Overall: I can't recommend this company if the family is important for you.

Pros: Salaries and benefits are generous
Cons: The working environment is bad, and everyone is under pressure to do more with less. Promotions are non-existent, people don't care anymore, everyone is looking to leave to find a place with a brighter future.  Cisco is so big that the highest levels of management doesn't have any idea what the worker bees are actually doing.  The people that are laid off don't make sense.  The company is completely fragmented with VPs creating their own fiefdoms.  Cisco used to be a fun and interesting place to work at, now everyone is too busy looking over their shoulders and taking credit for work they didn't do.

Pros:
Laid back, positive environment, decent salary, good manager, forgiving environment. Some times there are inevitable frustration and hard times but it quickly vents away. Great technologies to learn. 
Free ev charger.
Some of the cafeteria are decent.
Employees can go to any of the numerous building covering massive area any time (except lab) and sit anywhere and attend meeting or do whatever.
Cons:
Public newspaper says Cisco is getting fatter in the middle and need to get rid off excess mid level management. In some way, it might be true but also I saw talented and experienced engineers impacted and incompetent engineers have stayed. They really need to be careful in this respect because many many good employees have left during last year. More jobs are getting done by fewer employees as a result and quality suffers too. 

Encourages new ideas but quality/experiences takes a back seat. Quite a lot of times, there are turmoil

I feel like it is impossible to move within the company. Few other job inquiries resulted in no-reply.

Pros: Cisco provides good benefits (10 company holidays, 4 weeks PTO, 1 week volunteering time, 4.5% 401k match, ESPP, maternity/paternity leave, emergency time off), promotes a positive work environment and a healthy work-life balance, and encourages movement within the company (including being rather supportive of remote work arrangements).  The huge range of products provide opportunity for lateral movement.   The large size provides a degree of stability.  Salaries are good but not the highest in the industry.
Cons:
Cisco has traditionally operated as a number of quasi-independent Business Units. 
 Soft-qualities such as work-life balance, encouraging movement, and quality of management can vary significantly between Business Units.  That said, Chuck Robbins' Executive Leadership Team has been making a concerted effort to address problem areas.  Cisco grows by acquisition so a significant fraction of the innovation happens outside the company.  This also leads to relatively frequent layoffs of redundant divisions and attrition as acquired employees become fully vested and seek opportunities elsewhere.

Pros:
Cisco Systems is a great place to work and it is getting better. It's a huge company, so it's not all perfect, but when you take it all together you come up with some pretty compelling reasons why leaving the company would be hard to do.

Specifically, if you perform well and work hard, you'll be rewarded well. In recent years it seems that managers have directed more of the rewards to those on the team that contribute more. Makes working longer hours worth it.

Also, flexibility is a huge benefit in Cisco (remote work, flexible hours, etc). This depends on you and your manager, but if you are trustworthy and self-directed you are afforded much flexibility.
Cons: If you want Cisco to be a fun place to work, you'll need to create the fun. I'm not saying it can't be a fun place but it'll be up to you to organize events and get teammates together.

Pros:
- A great opprtunity to work with some serioulsy talented people, especially out in the regions
 - Benefits and salary are above the industry norm
 - Ability to expand your experience through different roles within the company, out in the regions and at HQ
Cons:
- You have to wonder how some people especially at corporate are still  in their roles.. they should have gone a long while ago,  while some of the hard working, talented individuals have either moved on, or will soon do so, due to high frustration levels.
 - Still an old boys club mentality at the top...
 - Many executives have been there too long... need to bring in some fresh blood and a new way of thinking.
 - Recently lost its way with too much restructuring... it is breeding discontentment and bad morale in a big way.
